blocks.text: Given a positive integer n, print a centered pyramid of stars with n rows, where row i contains n minus i leading spaces followed by 2 times i minus 1 stars, so every row is centered above the one below it and the whole shape widens symmetrically toward the base.

blocks.title: Analogy: A Real Pyramid Viewed from the Front
blocks.text: Picture an actual stone pyramid seen from directly in front. The very top is a single block, and every layer below it is centered under the one above, extending equally to the left and right. The odd, growing star counts, 1, 3, 5, 7, and so on, are exactly what keeps every row perfectly centered over the row above it.

blocks.caption: Row i is n minus i spaces followed by 2i minus 1 stars, centered

blocks.content: {"headers":["Row","Output","Why"],"rows":[["Row 1","   *","Row 1 has n minus i, which is 3, leading spaces and 2i minus 1, which is 1, star, a single centered star at the very top."],["Row 2","  ***","One fewer leading space and two more stars than the row above, since the star count always grows by 2 to stay odd."],["Row 3"," *****","Continuing the same pattern, one fewer space, two more stars, keeping the row centered under the base."],["Row 4","*******","The final, widest row, no leading spaces at all and 2 times 4 minus 1, which is 7, stars."]]}

blocks.text: No rows at all, so nothing is printed.
Before writing any code, it is worth pausing on exactly why the star count follows the odd sequence 1, 3, 5, 7, rather than a simpler sequence like 1, 2, 3, 4.

blocks.title: How Should We Think?
blocks.text:
Observation 1: For row i to look centered, it needs to extend the same distance to the left and to the right of some single middle column, and a row with an odd number of stars is the only shape that has one true middle position with equal stars on both sides.

Observation 2: Testing this against a tiny example confirms it: with 1 star there is trivially a center; growing to 3 stars adds exactly one star on each side of that center, keeping it centered; growing to 5 stars adds one more on each side again. Each step adds 2 stars, one per side, which is exactly why the formula is 2i minus 1 and not i or 2i.

Observation 3: The leading gap formula, n minus i, is the same shrinking gap already used in the left half pyramid, since it exists purely to push the star region toward the horizontal center as the pattern gets wider.

Observation 4: Once both formulas are known for row i, the shrinking gap and the odd, growing star count, the same direct-construction technique used everywhere else in this division still applies without any changes.
That reasoning is what turns "why is it 2i minus 1" from a memorized formula into something derivable from the centering requirement itself.

Use an outer loop for each row i, and an inner loop that checks every column this row actually uses, deciding for each one individually whether it still falls inside the leading gap or has reached the star region.

items: Loop over each row i from 1 to n.
Compute the gap size for this row, n minus i.
Check every column from 0 up to n plus i minus 2.
If the column is still within the gap, print a space, otherwise print a star.
After finishing a row, move to the next line.

blocks.caption: Brute force flow: check every column position and decide space or star

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: gap is computed once per row, using n minus i, before the inner loop begins, so the boundary between the space region and the star region is fixed once rather than re-derived on every column.
The inner loop's bound, n plus i minus 1, is exactly the total width this row uses, the gap plus the odd star count combined, so every column that matters gets checked exactly once.

The comparison j less than gap decides space or star for a single column at a time, even though this same boundary never moves within the row, which is exactly the inefficiency the optimized version removes.

blocks.text: This is correct, since every column position in every row is individually checked and assigned the right character, keeping each row centered above the next.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared), since the total stars across all rows is 1 plus 3 plus up to 2n minus 1, proportional to n squared, and every position is checked individually.
Space: O(1) extra space, no string is ever built.

Limitation: checking every column position one at a time wastes a per cell decision that never changes within a row, since both the gap size and the star count for row i are already known before the row even starts. Both regions can instead be built directly in one operation each, with no per cell checking at all.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why checking every column works but is wasteful: the same gap-versus-star boundary, fixed at column n minus i for the entire row, gets re-checked on every one of that row's columns instead of being used once.

What stays the same as other patterns in this division: the underlying insight, both region lengths, the gap and the stars, are known before the row starts, so both can be built directly.

What is different here compared to a plain, non centered pyramid: the star count must follow the odd sequence 2i minus 1, not the plain count i, in order to keep every row centered.

Can the same direct-construction technique be reused unchanged: yes, a repeat operation still builds each region in one step regardless of which formula, plain or odd, computed its length.

The core idea: build the shrinking gap directly at length n minus i, build the odd, growing star region directly at length 2i minus 1, concatenate them, then print the row once.

For each row i, build the leading gap and the star region directly, using one operation for the n minus i spaces and another for the 2i minus 1 stars, then concatenate them into a single row string. This removes all per cell branching, needing only one print call per row.
For each row i, build the leading gap and the odd star region directly, one operation each, then concatenate them into a single row string and print it once.

blocks.caption: Optimized flow: build the spaces and stars directly, one print call per row

blocks.text: This works because both of row i's region lengths, n minus i for the gap and 2i minus 1 for the stars, are fully known ahead of time; a direct repeat operation still constructs each region in one step, with no dependence on any other row. As i increases from 1 to n, the gap n minus i shrinks from n minus 1 down to 0, while the odd star count 2i minus 1 grows from 1 up to 2n minus 1, and concatenating the two produces exactly the right, centered row every time.

items: The gap length is computed as n minus i and the star length as 2 times i minus 1, directly inside the outer loop, so both formulas are evaluated once per row rather than once per column.

Two direct repeat operations construct the gap and the odd star region separately, exactly the same construction technique used everywhere else in this division, then concatenation joins them into the finished row.

Each row is printed immediately after being built, one output call per row, with both the shrinking gap and the odd growing star count handled entirely by their formulas, not by any special casing in the loop itself.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared) total characters produced, the same as the brute force, but with no per cell branching and only O(n) print calls instead of O(n squared) checks.
Space: O(n), for the single row string being built and printed at a time.
10. Further Optimization: A Single Output Call

Every row is already being built directly in one operation, so instead of printing each one separately, all n rows can be built first, joined together with newline characters, and the entire pattern can be produced with a single output call.

blocks.caption: Further optimization: join every row into one string and output it in a single call

items: Every row is still built directly from its own shrinking gap, n minus i, and odd, growing star count, 2i minus 1, exactly as in the optimized version, the only change is deferring output until every row exists.
Joining all n rows with newline characters assembles the complete centered pattern as a single string, entirely in memory, before any output call happens.
A single print call at the very end outputs the whole pyramid, cutting the operation count down to exactly 1 regardless of how large n is.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared), the same total characters produced.
Space: O(n squared), to hold every row joined into one string before the single output call. This trades some memory for the fewest possible output calls, exactly one, no matter how large n is.

blocks.text: A centered pyramid is really just two formulas combined, a shrinking gap and a growing, always odd, star count. Odd numbers are what let each row stay perfectly centered under the one above, since an odd count always has one middle position with equal room on both sides.

items: Using an even star count formula like 2i instead of 2i minus 1, which breaks the centering entirely.
Mixing up the gap formula with the one used for a plain, non centered pyramid.
Forgetting the n = 0 edge case, where nothing at all should be printed.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","Expected Behavior"],"rows":[["n = 0","Produces an empty pattern with no output, since there are no rows to build."],["n = 1","The smallest non-empty pyramid, a single centered star, since n minus i is 0 and 2i minus 1 is 1 when both n and i are 1."]]}

blocks.text: Deriving the odd star count formula, 2i minus 1, by simply testing it against a small example like n = 3 before writing any code is a fast way to avoid an off by one mistake that is very easy to make with centered patterns.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text:
If the interviewer says "why must the star count be odd", think: an odd count is the only one with a true middle position and equal stars on both sides of it.
If the interviewer says "can you avoid checking every column", think: build the shrinking gap and the odd star region directly, using their known lengths.
If the interviewer says "can you reduce this to one output call", think: build every row first, join with newlines, print once.

The left half pyramid, whose shrinking gap formula, n minus i, reappears here unchanged.
The right half pyramid, whose growing star count, i, becomes the odd, growing star count 2i minus 1 here, to achieve centering.
The inverted full pyramid, which mirrors this shape top to bottom the same way the inverted half pyramids mirror their own counterparts.
Diamond patterns, which stack a full pyramid and its inverted mirror to form a single centered shape.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: All three versions produce the same O(n squared) total characters, since that is fixed by the shape itself. What changes is how that output is organized: per cell checks in the brute force version, one formula built row per print call in the optimized version, and exactly one call for the entire pattern in the further optimized version.

items: Pattern: pattern printing that combines a shrinking gap with an odd, symmetrically growing star region, the shape that makes each row visually centered above the next.

Core Idea: row i always needs exactly n minus i spaces and 2i minus 1 stars, both lengths known before that row is built, so two direct repeat operations construct each region in one step, and joining every row allows a single output call.
Time: O(n squared) checks for the brute force, O(n) output calls for the optimized version, O(1) for the further optimized version; total characters printed are always O(n squared).
Space: O(1) extra for the brute force, O(n) for the current row, O(n squared) for the fully joined pattern.
Most Important Observation: centering a growing shape is not a new algorithm, it is the same known-length direct construction, fed an odd star count formula instead of a plain one.
Interview Difficulty: easy to produce the correct shape by trial and error; explaining why the star count must be odd is what shows real understanding of centering.
One line memory trick: shrinking gap n minus i, odd growing stars 2i minus 1, build both directly and concatenate.
